extracted.intended_audience: secondary-school students preparing for the China Mathematical Olympiad, their coaches, and contest organizers
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, format, and problem constraints appearing in the China Mathematical Olympiad contest booklet (problem statements, definitions, and scheduling information). Useful for contestants and coaches preparing for the contest and for reproducing/understanding problem constraints exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition duration and problem load
rubrics_metrics.description: The competition lasts for 2 days, and there are 3 problems to be completed within 4.5 hours each day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the time allotment per exam session and the number of problems per session; solutions should be prepared with that time-pressure in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical number of participants / eligibility note
rubrics_metrics.description: About 150 winners of the China Mathematical Competition take part in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the scale of the China Mathematical Olympiad and implies selection/qualification from earlier rounds (not a precise eligibility rubric but contextual information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exam session scheduling (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example session times given in the booklet: e.g., 'First Day 8:00-12:30 January 15, 2003' and similar day schedules such as '8:30-13:00 January 8, 2004'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows actual historical time windows used for contest administration; useful for logistical planning and expected session lengths (4.5 or 4.5 hours / 4.5–4.5+).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: escribed circle / escenter
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark : The circle which is tangent to one side of a triangle and two other extended sides is called an escribed circle. The center of an escribed circle is called an escenter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition and terminology when solving or writing geometry solutions involving excircles; appears in a geometry problem and is accepted vocabulary in solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary hiring policy (problem rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first 3 applicants should not be employed. From the fourth onward an applicant will be compared with the preceding ones. If he exceeds in ability all the proceedings applicants, he will be employed. Otherwise he will not, and the interview goes on. If the preceding nine persons are not employed, the last one will be employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the exact procedural rule used to define the combinatorial/probability problem about the interviewer’s policy; any solution must respect these selection rules when counting permutations or probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set S constraints (mutual coprime / common-divisor conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume that S satisfies: (1) every element in S is a positive integer and not greater than 100; (2) for any two different elements a and b in S, there is an element c in S such that gcd(a,c)=1 and gcd(b,c)=1; (3) for any two different elements a and b in S, there is an element d, different from a and b, such that gcd(a,d)>1 and gcd(b,d)>1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three conditions are the precise constraints of the number-theory problem asking for the maximum cardinality of S; any construction or upper bound must satisfy all three simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-set M constraints for convex polygon problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be a set consisting of n points in the plane, and satisfying: (1) there exist 7 points in M which constitute the vertices of a convex heptagon; (2) if for any 5 points in M which constitute the vertices of a convex pentagon, then there is a point in M which lies in the interior of the pentagon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two conditions are the exact combinatorial-geometric constraints for the problem asking the minimal n; constructions and proofs must adhere to both conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence definition with floor function
rubrics_metrics.description: Let c be a positive integer, and a number sequence x1, x2, ... satisfy x1 = c and (recurrence involving the floor function) where [x] denotes the largest integer not greater than x. Determine x_n in terms of n and c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the recurrence formula is given in the booklet (truncated here), the key constraints are initial value x1 = c and use of the floor operator [x]; solutions classify x_n depending on c (mod 3) and must respect integer-floor behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic constraint problem: positive variables and linear relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume positive numbers a, b, c, x, y, z satisfy cy + bz = a; az + cx = b; bx + ay = c. Find the minimum value of the function f(x,y,z) = x^2/(1+x) + y^2/(1+y) + z^2/(1+z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All variables are positive and satisfy the three linear relations; valid approaches in solutions use these equalities (e.g., interpreting x,y,z as cosines of triangle angles) to reduce and minimize f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry problem hypothesis: incenter, orthocenter, midpoints and collinearity criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose points I and H are the incenter and orthocenter of an acute triangle ABC respectively, and points B1 and C1 are the midpoints of sides AC and AB respectively. It is known that ray B1I intersects side AB at B2 (B2 ≠ B) and ray C1I intersects the extension of AC at C2; B2C2 and BC intersect at K and A1 is the circumcenter of ABHC. Prove that three points A, I and A1 are collinear if and only if the areas of ABKB2 and ACKC2 are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the exact hypothesis and required equivalence for the geometry problem: solutions must use these point definitions and area equality to show the collinearity equivalence (and rely on established geometry facts stated in the booklet).
